uncited: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) is a higher-order numerical integration method for volume rendering that queries the vector field at four distinct positions to compute a single ray step, significantly reducing truncation error compared to the zero-order [Rectangle Rule](2082-zero-order-integration-rectangle-rule.md) and first-order [Euler Integration](3839-runge-kutta-2-3-ode-solver.md) methods.
It sets itself apart by achieving an error order of $O(dt^5)$ per step, allowing for larger step sizes while maintaining accuracy, though it requires four texture lookups per step rather than one.
*   **Input:** Current position $x_n$ (or $x_i$), step size $dt$ (or $\delta$), and optionally a time parameter $t_{\text{func}}$ for unsteady fields.
The method computes four intermediate slopes ($k_1$ through $k_4$ or $v_0$ through $v_3$) and combines them with specific weights.
A first-order integrator that uses only the current position and vector field value to compute the next step ($x_{n+1} = x_n + dt \cdot v(x_n)$).
It is used when performance is critical and accuracy requirements are low.
*   **When to use:** When visual accuracy of streamlines or particle paths is more important than raw performance, or when large step sizes are needed to cover long distances without excessive error.

*   **When not to use:** When real-time performance is the primary constraint and the vector field is simple or low-resolution, or when adaptive step sizing is required (in which case RK2/3 might be preferred).
The Runge-Kutta methods were developed by Carl Runge and Martin Wilhelm Kutta in the early 20th century.
In the context of volume rendering and vector field visualization, RK4 is widely used as a standard high-order integrator for streamlines and pathlines.
The method is preferred over Euler integration when the visual fidelity of the flow topology is critical.
